title: The web: HTTP, REST, cookies, CORS, TLS
note: HTTP is a request–response protocol. A safe method does not change server state; an idempotent method has the same effect whether sent once or many times. Status codes are grouped by first digit: 1xx informational, 2xx success, 3xx redirection, 4xx client error, 5xx server error.

read.title: One request, many rules
text: When a browser loads a page, it sends an HTTP request with a method, a path, and headers, and the server answers with a status code, headers, and usually a body. Methods carry promises. GET and HEAD are safe, meaning they should not change anything on the server. PUT and DELETE are not safe but are idempotent: sending the same request twice leaves the server in the same state as sending it once. POST makes neither promise, which is why browsers warn before resubmitting a form.

Caching headers let a response be reused. Cache-Control: max-age says how long a stored copy stays fresh. Once it goes stale, the browser can revalidate by sending the stored ETag in If-None-Match; if nothing changed, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body.

Browsers also guard users across sites. The same-origin policy stops a script from one origin, meaning scheme, host, and port, from reading responses from another. CORS is the server's way to relax that rule by naming origins it trusts. Cookies carry flags of their own: Secure limits them to HTTPS, HttpOnly hides them from scripts, and SameSite controls whether they ride along on cross-site requests. Underneath it all, TLS encrypts the connection and proves the server's identity with a certificate.
